plan.strategy: Establish the measured baseline with the seed implementation (flat gather kernel + cached direct launcher for the last-dim contiguous case, generic stride kernel otherwise), with alias protection re-expressed as a metadata byte-range overlap test because torch._C._is_alias_of is rejected by candidate admission.

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker (5/5 attempts: batch of 4 workloads at metrics level, one workload at metrics level, one workload at instruction level). capabilities=[], artifacts=[], metrics={} on every attempt; only request/result manifests were written, which the recorder does not accept as evidence artifacts.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline of the seed candidate. The flat last-dim path costs ~0.69x on all large/mid cases (timing-2 fp16 1.6996ms vs 1.1738ms reference; timing-8 fp32 1.7125ms vs 1.1402ms) while the 1024x3 cases are launch-overhead bound at 0.79-0.93x. Reference latency is essentially dtype-independent per element (1.174ms fp16 vs 1.140ms fp32 for the same 3.1M elements), so the kernel is per-element bound, not byte bound.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Bounded target-side diagnostics isolated the mechanism: a pure copy of the same footprint is 0.0682ms, four misaligned shifted loads are 0.0672ms, but adding only `lane % 3` raises it to 2.171ms and the seed's four tl.gather shuffles cost ~0.41ms each. Replace the integer modulo with an fp32-reciprocal phase and the four gathers with eight shifted contiguous loads: the correct formula then runs at 0.0752ms for 1M vectors.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Integer `%` and `//` on a per-lane tile are scalarized by this backend and cost ~32x a pure copy; `tl.gather` costs ~6x; misaligned and negatively-offset contiguous loads are free. Probe such primitives with bounded target jobs before choosing a formulation.

plan.strategy: Eliminate the two primitives that scalarize on this backend (integer per-lane modulo for the phase, tl.gather for the permutation) from the contiguous last-dim path, keeping the same arithmetic expression and operand order so results are bit-identical to the seed for every stored lane.
plan.code_changes: Flat kernel: replaced `phase = lane % 3` with a modulo-free phase (`lane - 3*(lane*0.3333333432674408 -> int32)`) and replaced the four tl.gather permutations with eight plain shifted contiguous loads (n-2, n-1, n+1, n+2 for both inputs) plus a 2-level tl.where select over three precomputed products t0/t1/t2. Store/load masks unchanged in kind. Added shape[dim]==3 and other.dtype==input.dtype to the flat-path condition. General ND path, plan cache, raw launcher and alias guard untouched.
plan.hypothesis: The flat path is bound by scalarized per-lane `%`/gather code, not by bytes: on the target, copy=0.067 ms and 4 misaligned loads=0.067 ms per 1M vectors, but adding only `lane % 3` costs 2.171 ms and the 4 gathers ~1.66 ms, while the fully correct modulo-free 8-load version measures 0.0752 ms with max_abs_err 0.0078 (fp16) / 0.0 (fp32).

expected_effect.mechanism: Removes the two primitives that scalarize on this backend (per-lane integer modulo and tl.gather), leaving only contiguous DMA loads and one select network, so the 1M-vector cases should drop from 1.70 ms to near the 0.068-0.075 ms copy floor measured for the same footprint.

conclusion.root_cause: The seed's flat kernel was bound by two primitives that this backend lowers to scalar-ish code: the per-lane integer modulo used to build the phase pattern (a single `lane % 3` over a 2048-lane tile costs 2.171ms per 1M vectors versus 0.068ms for a pure copy) and four tl.gather shuffles (~0.41ms each). Misaligned and negatively-offset contiguous loads are free (0.067ms for four shifted loads), so replacing the permutation with eight shifted loads and deriving the phase from an fp32 reciprocal plus a truncating cast removes essentially all of that overhead; the remaining cost for sub-200k-element cases is host dispatch, not the device kernel.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Prediction was that the 1M-vector cases would fall from 1.70ms to near the 0.068-0.075ms copy floor if the modulo and gather were the limiters; observed 0.0808ms (timing-2, fp16, 14.50x), 0.0998ms (timing-5, 11.73x) and 0.1489ms (timing-8, fp32, 7.64x), so the mechanism is confirmed and the fp16 large case is within 19% of the 0.0682ms floor measured for the same footprint. The mid cases exceeded the prediction: 65536x3 dropped to 0.0251-0.0256ms (3.51-4.06x) because they are now pure host-dispatch bound, matching the cost of the 3072-element cases. The 1M fp32 case is 26% above its own 0.1179ms floor, consistent with 8 fp32 streams at BLOCK=1024 having a tighter UB budget than the fp16 path. Small cases show a lower speedup than the baseline (0.930 -> 0.771 for timing-0) only because the reference latency was measured lower this round (0.0247 vs 0.0193ms); their absolute candidate latency improved from 0.02657 to 0.02509ms and they are launch-floor bound, not kernel bound.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Two remaining levers. (1) Host dispatch: every timing case with <=196k elements now sits at a ~25.1us walltime floor (timing-0/3/6 = 0.0251/0.0259/0.0253ms, timing-1/4/7 = 0.0251/0.0256/0.0253ms), i.e. the same cost as the 3072-element cases, so the wrapper (alias overlap checks, shape/dtype comparisons, dict plan lookup keyed on a.device.index, stream query) rather than the kernel dominates 6 of 9 timing cases; measure and trim it. (2) Close the residual gap to the measured copy floor on the large cases: fp16 1M is 0.0808ms against a 0.0682ms floor (+19%) and fp32 1M is 0.1489ms against 0.1179ms (+26%), where a cheaper combine or BLOCK tuning may recover part of the gap.

Sub-100us cases are then bound purely by host dispatch, so wrapper cost becomes the next bottleneck.

plan.strategy: Retune the flat-kernel tile width for the three device-bound 1M-vector cases so each program carries the widest UB-resident tile that still fits.
plan.code_changes: `_pick_block` now returns 4096 for 2-byte dtypes and 2048 for 4-byte dtypes when n_elem > 131072 (previously 2048/1024); the <=131072 branch is unchanged at 1024. Kernel body, masks, launch path and general ND path untouched.
plan.hypothesis: The large cases are now limited by per-program overhead and stream depth rather than by bytes or by the select network: on identical inputs, fp16 1M improves 1024->2048->4096 as 0.1435/0.0842/0.0689 ms and fp32 1M improves 512->1024->2048 as 0.2661/0.1531/0.0962 ms, so the widest tile that fits UB (4096 fp16 / 2048 fp32) should take timing-2 from 0.0808 toward 0.069 ms and timing-8 from 0.1489 toward 0.096 ms.

expected_effect.mechanism: A wider tile amortizes per-program prologue/DMA setup over more elements and keeps eight in-flight streams per program, cutting device time on the three 1M-vector cases toward the measured copy floor.

conclusion.root_cause: Per-program prologue and stream-setup overhead, not bytes or the phase-select network, limited the three 1M-vector cases: with BLOCK widened to 4096 (2-byte) / 2048 (4-byte) the same kernel body drops from 0.0842 to 0.0689ms (fp16 debug) and from 0.1531 to 0.0962ms (fp32 debug), and the authoritative run confirmed 0.0537/0.0924ms. Every workload at or below 196608 elements is now dominated by the ~24us host launch path.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted timing-2 0.0808 -> ~0.069ms and timing-8 0.1489 -> ~0.096ms from the measured BLOCK sweep; observed 0.0537ms (21.80x, better than predicted) and 0.0924ms (12.31x, essentially as predicted). timing-5 improved 11.73x -> 16.30x (0.0998 -> 0.0718ms). Aggregate geo_mean rose 3.1675 -> 3.7214 (+17.5%), close to the ~3.6-3.7 predicted from the sweep. The mid cases also improved slightly (0.0251 -> 0.0238ms) because fewer programs reduced device time, but they remain at the same level as the 3072-element cases, confirming that they are host-dispatch bound rather than kernel bound. The small cases stayed at 0.79-0.80x because their reference latency is ~0.019ms and our ~0.0236ms is almost entirely launch overhead.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Host dispatch is now the dominant cost for 6 of 9 timing cases: the 3072-element cases (0.02369/0.02356ms, 0.79-0.80x) and the 65536-vector cases (0.02353-0.02399ms, 3.76-4.37x) all sit at the same ~23.6-24.0us walltime, which matches the Python wrapper overhead measured on the target (run() 0.0302ms versus a bare raw-launch floor of 0.0161ms on the same tensors, i.e. ~14us of metadata work per call). Cache the resolved flat plan behind a cheap pointer+numel+dtype fast path so the repeated-call path does no shape/contiguity/alias metadata work. Separately, the 1M-vector cases are at 0.0537ms (fp16) and 0.0924ms (fp32); a wider tile (8192 fp16 / 4096 fp32) is the next thing to price for those.
conclusion.debug_lesson: The copy floor measured at BLOCK=2048 (0.0682ms) was not the real floor: a wider tile beats it (0.0537ms at BLOCK=4096), so tile width must be swept at the largest size actually reachable, not inferred from a small-tile control.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Architecture is settled (modulo-free phase, shifted contiguous loads); the work has moved to per-program tiling and now to host-dispatch cost, since six of nine timing cases are launch bound.

plan.strategy: Move validation and plan resolution out of the steady-state launch path, and close the one-sided mask defect that made the flat path read past the tensor end.
plan.code_changes: (1) Perf: run() gained a single-entry fast path that memoizes the resolved flat dispatch as (pa, pb, po, n_elem, out.dtype, entry, device_index) and revalidates it with three data_ptr comparisons, one numel and one dtype identity check, then launches through the cached raw launcher, skipping alias tests, shape/contiguity/dtype validation, the plan dict lookup and the device-index query; mismatch falls back to the unchanged slow path. (2) Safety: the two backward neighbor streams are now masked on both sides (added & (base < n_elem)) so lanes inside the tile but past the tensor never read up to a tile width beyond its end. Kernel arithmetic, tiling and the general ND path unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: Six of nine timing workloads are bound by Python-side dispatch rather than by the device kernel: on the target run() costs 0.0302ms (small) and 0.0242ms (mid) while the identical raw launch with everything precomputed costs 0.0161/0.0104ms, i.e. ~14us of per-call metadata work; removing it should lift the 3072-element cases from 0.79-0.80x toward ~1.2x and the 65536-vector cases from 3.76-4.37x toward ~5-7x, leaving the 1M cases unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: Collapses the steady-state per-call host work from ~20 tensor metadata accesses to 5, so launch-bound workloads (~24us walltime) approach the measured bare raw-launch floor of ~10-16us.

key_params.memo: (pa, pb, po, n_elem, dtype, entry, device_index)

conclusion.root_cause: Repeated-call dispatch cost, not device work, bound every workload at or below 196608 elements: run() re-read ~20 pieces of tensor metadata (data_ptr, numel, element_size, shape comparisons, contiguity flags, device index, dict key with device.index) on every invocation, costing ~14us on top of a 10-16us raw launch. Memoizing the resolved flat dispatch behind three pointer comparisons plus numel and dtype brings those workloads to 13.4-14.3us. The same edit exposed a one-sided mask defect (backward streams bounded only below) which is also fixed and verified on tensors down to 1 vector.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted the small cases would go 0.79-0.80x -> ~1.2x and the mid cases 3.76-4.37x -> ~5-7x while the 1M cases stayed put. Observed: small 1.315/1.269/1.256x (latency 0.0242/0.0237/0.0236 -> 0.01355/0.01426/0.01404ms), mid 6.707/6.534/7.335x (0.0238/0.0238/0.0235 -> 0.01339/0.01375/0.01401ms), and the 1M cases unchanged within noise (0.0537 -> 0.0533, 0.0718 -> 0.0712, 0.0924 -> 0.0930ms). The floor fell to ~14.0us against a measured bare raw-launch floor of 10.4-16.1us, so the ~14us of recoverable wrapper work was largely removed and about 2-3us of validation remains. Aggregate geo_mean rose 3.7214 -> 5.2392 (+40.8%) and min_speedup rose 0.787 -> 1.256, i.e. every workload now beats the reference.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three 1M-vector cases are now the only device-bound ones (timing-2 0.0533ms/21.96x, timing-5 0.0712ms/16.44x, timing-8 0.0930ms/12.23x) while every other workload sits at a 13.4-14.3us host floor. Measured follow-ups: fp32 BLOCK 2048->4096 improves 1M fp32 from 0.0964 to 0.0718ms, bf16 fp32-arithmetic is worse (0.0932 vs 0.0742) so native bf16 math stays, and fp16 BLOCK=8192 does not compile. So widen the 4-byte tile to 4096 and then stop: further wrapper trimming can recover at most ~3us of the ~10-16us bare-launch floor.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Two host-side facts dominated the launch-bound workloads: the steady-state wrapper was costing ~14us of tensor metadata work per call, and the raw launcher requires packed_metadata as its sixth argument (passing a scalar there segfaults the worker). A one-sided mask on a backward stream is also unsafe: lanes inside a tile but past the tensor read up to a whole tile beyond its end, which is invisible for large tensors and fatal for tiny ones.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Device work is essentially done for 6 of 9 timing cases; the remaining gains are confined to the three 1M-vector cases, where the kernel is 12-22x faster than the reference but still above its own floor.

plan.strategy: Raise the 4-byte tile to the widest width the 2-byte path already uses and the compiler accepts.
plan.code_changes: `_pick_block` now returns 4096 for every element size above the 131072-element threshold (previously 2048 for 4-byte elements); the <=131072 branch is unchanged at 1024. Kernel body, masks, fast path and general ND path untouched.
plan.hypothesis: The 1M-vector fp32 case is still paying per-program overhead because its tile is half as wide as the 2-byte one: on identical inputs fp32 1M measures 2048 -> 0.0964 ms and 4096 -> 0.0718 ms, and an fp16 tile at 8192 does not compile, so 4096 is the widest tile both element sizes tolerate. timing-8 should improve from 0.0930 ms toward 0.072 ms, with fp16/bf16 and the host-bound cases essentially unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: A wider 4-byte tile amortizes per-program prologue over twice as many elements, cutting the fp32 1M-vector device time toward the 2-byte value.

profile.summary: failed: msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker

conclusion.root_cause: The 4-byte large case was still paying per-program prologue because its tile was half as wide as the 2-byte one; widening it to 4096 (the widest the compiler accepts, since fp16 at 8192 fails to compile) cut fp32 1M device time from 0.0930 to 0.0682ms. The same widening over-tiled the 196608-element fp32 case, where 48 programs on 20 cores leave a partial third wave.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Predicted timing-8 0.0930 -> ~0.072ms from the measured 2048-vs-4096 comparison; observed 0.0682ms (16.67x versus 12.23x), better than predicted. But the same change also applied to the fp32 mid case, whose grid fell from 96 to 48 programs: timing-7 went 0.01401 -> 0.01524ms (7.335x -> 6.742x) and timing-6 0.01404 -> 0.01533ms, both consistent with a 2.4-wave grid no longer hiding under the ~14us host floor. The 2-byte mid cases were unaffected (0.01395/0.01399ms) because their tile width did not change. Aggregate geo_mean rose 5.2392 -> 5.4911 (+4.8%), less than a clean timing-8-only gain would have given, and min_speedup rose 1.256 -> 1.309.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Fix the tile ladder to respect wave count (block <= n/80, i.e. 1024 below 32768 elements, 2048 up to 262144, 4096 above), which should restore timing-7 from 0.01524 to ~0.0140ms (6.74x -> ~7.3x) while keeping timing-8 at 0.0682ms. Also price a lower-op-count select form (select the four operands, then two multiplies and one subtract = 7 vector ops, instead of three products plus two selects = 11) since timing-5 shows bf16 arithmetic, not bytes, is the limiter there (0.0707ms bf16 versus 0.0528ms fp16 for the same footprint).
conclusion.debug_lesson: Tile width must be chosen against available parallelism, not just UB capacity: at 196608 elements a 4096-wide tile leaves only 48 programs on 20 cores (2.4 waves) and becomes device-bound at ~15.2us, whereas 2048 gives 96 programs and stays hidden under the ~14us host floor.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Tile width is now tuned at the ceiling for the largest case; the next step is to make the ladder wave-aware so mid sizes keep their parallelism, and to cut vector ALU ops for the bf16 case that is ALU-limited rather than byte-limited.

view.title: cross_out 优化轨迹
view.subtitle: 历史 KGS 参考 · 本批 5 次正式评测

plan.strategy: Replace the inherited FlagGems cross wrapper with two purpose-built Triton kernels: a flat contiguous kernel for the dominant last-axis layout (eight shifted contiguous block loads + four selects reproduce aten's cross arithmetic with no gather) and a generic (outer,3,inner) kernel for arbitrary cross axis / strides / broadcasting.
plan.code_changes: New self-contained tmp/main.py: _cross_flat_kernel over the flat 3*N index space using only +1/+2/-1/-2 shifted contiguous loads and per-lane column selection; _cross_general_kernel with six slice loads and three slice stores; wrapper resolves dim (incl. dim=None first-size-3 rule), validates dtype/shape/device and resizes out like the aten out-variant.
plan.hypothesis: The inherited FlagGems path is far off the roofline (geo_mean 0.136, i.e. ~7x slower than the aten reference) because it pays host-side validation plus a general strided kernel. A dedicated flat kernel with fully contiguous accesses should move all nine timing workloads toward the memory roofline.

expected_effect.mechanism: First measured round of a dedicated flat Triton cross kernel; establishes the reference point for later tuning.

conclusion.root_cause: Baseline round. The inherited FlagGems path measured geo_mean 0.136 (every timing case below 1.0). The new dedicated flat kernel lifted geo_mean to 0.4975 with all 21 workloads numerically correct, but bounded diagnostics showed the flat kernel itself is bound neither by bytes nor by loads: 1M rows of fp16 and fp32 both take ~1.70 ms, i.e. ~20 core-cycles per element, while an aligned copy of the same element count takes 0.065-0.074 ms. Diagnostics also showed that eight shifted (+1/+2/-1/-2) contiguous loads with one affine mask reach 0.078 ms, so the per-lane `off % 3` phase computation plus the four distinct per-load boolean masks are what force the backend onto a scalar path.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline, so no prior measurement to compare against. Workload-level picture versus the 0.1357 starting KPI: all 9 timing cases passed but only the two 65536-row cases and the three 1048576-row cases exceeded 0.66x, while the three 1024x3 cases reached only 0.248-0.259x. Two independent limits were quantified by bounded diagnostics: (a) device kernel - the flat kernel needs ~1.70 ms for 1M rows where the aligned-copy ceiling is 0.073 ms, a ~23x gap caused by the runtime modulo phase; (b) host dispatch - an empty Triton launch costs ~60.5 us walltime while the plain Python wrapper arithmetic costs only 6.1 us, and the aten reference performs the whole 1024x3 cross in ~19 us, so the three smallest cases are almost entirely host-overhead bound and cap the geo_mean regardless of device speed.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Replace the runtime `off % 3` phase with a compile-time constant pattern by making every program's flat base a multiple of 3 (STEP = BLOCK - BLOCK % 3, phase = arange % 3), keeping the same eight plain-affine shifted loads, then separately attack the ~60 us Triton host dispatch overhead that dominates the three 1024x3 cases.
conclusion.debug_lesson: On this Ascend backend only plain-affine block indices lower to block DMA: `tl.minimum`/`tl.maximum` index clamps cost 70x (5.5-7.3 ms vs 0.078 ms) and 2-D strided tiles cost 130x (10.1 ms). Load count is nearly free (4/6/8 shifted loads all ~0.078 ms), so tiling decisions should target index-expression simplicity, not byte volume.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Started from the FlagGems seed (0.136). Moved to a self-contained pair of Triton kernels (flat last-axis kernel + generic (outer,3,inner) kernel) for a 0.4975 geo_mean baseline. Bounded microbenchmarks then redirected the effort from bandwidth/tiling toward (i) index-expression lowering and (ii) host dispatch overhead, which the device-side roofline alone would not have revealed.
